result.markdown: --- title: "Relationships" --- ::: {.callout-tip} #### Learning objectives - Use scatter plots to explore the relationship between two numeric variables. - Deal with skewed variables and overplotting. - Add trend lines, and use a third variable without overloading the plot. ::: ::: {.hero} ![Income against life expectancy for 167 countries, with one region highlighted. We build towards figures like this.](images/highlight_after.png){width=60%} ::: ## Load packages and data We use the Gapminder data for 2010: one row per country. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv") ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from plotnine import * gapminder = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv") ``` ::: ::: ## The scatter plot Core A scatter plot puts one variable on each axis and draws one point per observation. It is the default choice when you ask "does one thing go with another?" ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy")) + geom_point()) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: Most countries are squashed into the left of the plot, because a few very rich countries stretch the x axis. Income is a classic *skewed* variable. ## Log scales for skewed data Core On a log scale, each step along the axis is a multiplication rather than an addition: 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000. This spreads out the crowded low values. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) + geom_point() + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy")) + geom_point() + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: The relationship now looks close to a straight line: each doubling of income is associated with a similar gain in life expectancy. ::: {.callout-important} #### Design principle: say when an axis is on a log scale Many readers assume a linear axis. Write "log scale" in the axis label, and use readable tick labels such as $1,000 rather than 3. ::: ## Overplotting Core When points overlap, dense areas look the same as sparse ones. Transparency (`alpha`) helps: overlapping points build up darker areas. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) + geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.4, colour = "#003E72") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy")) + geom_point(size=2.5, alpha=0.4, color="#003E72") + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: With thousands of points, consider `geom_bin_2d()` or `geom_hex()`, which count points in small tiles, or a density contour. ## Trend lines Core `geom_smooth()` adds a fitted line. `method = "lm"` fits a straight line; the default in R is a flexible curve (loess), which is useful for spotting non-linear patterns. The grey band is a confidence interval for the fitted line. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#D6083B") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy")) + geom_point(alpha=0.4) + geom_smooth(method="lm", color="#D6083B") + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: A trend line is a model. Only add one if it helps the message, and say what kind of line it is in the legend or caption. This course is about showing relationships; to calculate and test them, see [Core statistics 3: correlations](https://cambiotraining.github.io/corestats/materials/cs3_practical_correlations.html). ## Adding a third variable Core Colour is the most common way to add a grouping variable. With six regions, though, the plot quickly becomes hard to read: six colours to tell apart and a legend to decode. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, colour = region)) + geom_point(size = 2) + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", color="region")) + geom_point(size=2) + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: Two better options, depending on the message: 1. **Highlight one group** and make the rest grey. This is covered in [Colour with purpose](colour.qmd). 2. **Split into small multiples**, one panel per group, using `facet_wrap()`. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) + geom_point(data = select(gapminder, -region), colour = "grey85", size = 1.2) + geom_point(colour = "#0072CF", size = 1.5) + facet_wrap(~ region) + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} background = gapminder.drop(columns="region") p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy")) + geom_point(data=background, color="#D9D9D9", size=1.2) + geom_point(color="#0072CF", size=1.5) + facet_wrap("region") + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)") + theme(figure_size=(7, 5))) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: The trick here is the first layer. It uses a copy of the data with the region column removed, so `facet_wrap()` cannot split it, and every panel shows *all* the countries in light grey. Each region is then drawn on top in blue, compared against the whole world. ## Exercises ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Children and child mortality {{< level 1 >}} Plot the number of children per woman (x) against child mortality (y). Is a log scale useful for either axis? Add a sensible title. ::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"} ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = children_per_woman, y = child_mortality)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + scale_y_log10() + labs(title = "Where women have more children, more children die young", x = "Children per woman", y = "Child deaths per 1,000 births (log scale)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="children_per_woman", y="child_mortality")) + geom_point(alpha=0.6) + scale_y_log10() + labs(title="Where women have more children, more children die young", x="Children per woman", y="Child deaths per 1,000 births (log scale)")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: Child mortality is skewed, so a log scale on y spreads out the low values. Children per woman is not strongly skewed, so a linear axis is fine. Be careful with the headline: this is a correlation across countries, not evidence that one causes the other. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Size as a channel {{< level 2 >}} Map `population` to point size in the income and life expectancy plot. What does it add? What problems does it introduce? ::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"} ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, size = population)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#003E72") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) + scale_size_area(max_size = 15, guide = "none") + labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-3.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", size="population")) + geom_point(alpha=0.5, color="#003E72") + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks]) + scale_size_area(max_size=15) + guides(size=None) + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")) p.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](relationships_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: Size shows which countries affect the most people. But area is a channel we read inaccurately, large bubbles hide small ones, and you need a legend to decode it. Use it for a rough impression, not for precise comparisons. `scale_size_area()` makes the bubble area, rather than its radius, proportional to the value, which is the honest choice. ::: ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-tip} #### Key points - Scatter plots are the default for relationships between two numeric variables. - Use a log scale for skewed variables, and label it clearly. - Transparency reduces overplotting. - A trend line is a model: add it only when it supports the message. - With many groups, highlight one or use small multiples instead of many colours. :::
